13.0.0.en: 1 "Lo, mine eye hath seen all this, mine ear hath heard and understood it. 2 What ye know, the same do I know also: I am not inferior unto you. 3 Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God."

13.0.1.en: Lo, mine eye hath seen all this,

13.0.2.en: mine ear hath heard and understood it [1].

13.0.3.en: * See how, even in his humility, what he proclaimed was symbolic, led by the prophetic Spirit, who reveals to him what is higher. For he says, "Mine eye hath seen all this"; it is clear that he speaks a prophetic vision. "Mine ear hath heard it": the one whom God finds holy He chooses to hear His mysteries.

13.0.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "And understood it"... When something is seen or heard about without understanding being granted to the man, it is no longer a prophetic vision. Pharaoh saw in a dream things that were to happen to Egypt, but he could not understand what he saw, and he was not a prophet. King Belshazzar saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall, yet he was not a prophet, because he did not obtain the understanding of what he saw.

13.0.6.en: What ye know, the same do I know also:

13.1.0.en: I am not inferior unto you [2].

13.1.1.en: The humble Job was obliged to defend himself and to praise himself, as the Apostle Paul did later, when some groups in Corinth made the accusation that he was not an apostle.

13.1.2.en: Here Job affirms that he is not inferior to them, and that what they know he knew also; in these circumstances he does not need sermons and discussions, but love, care and prayers to support him.

13.1.3.en: * May we not be strenuous in debate and slothful in our prayers (for them). Let us pray, dear beloved, let us pray that God may give us grace, even for our enemies, and especially for our brethren and loved ones.

13.2.0.en: St. Augustine Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God [3].

13.2.1.en: He turned away from his friends and turned toward God, for he found no rest in speaking with them; therefore he wanted to speak with the Almighty, for to be judged before God is better than to fall into the hand of a man. To enter into dialogue with God is easier than dialogue with friends. As David said to Gad the prophet: "I am in a great strait: let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man" (2 Sam 24:14; 1 Chr 21:13).

13.2.2.en: * I also know the infinite greatness of God, the unlimited wisdom of the Creator, and His amazing power; but with this knowledge [I desire to speak to the Lord], for I know His righteousness. Since He is righteous, He bears with those who speak with Him without being accused. For if He does not wish this, I will be silent, since I know what I am bound to as one who receives the honor of being His servant. By His command "I speak," and I dare to the point of accusing God.

13.2.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * I will not cease speaking with God, for am I speaking with a man? I speak with God, who knows the secrets of my thoughts.

13.2.4.en: He says that it is a matter of great value to be judged before God rather than to be judged before them.

13.2.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * We speak to the Almighty when we ask for His tenderness, and we argue with Him (are judged before God) when we unite with Him in His righteousness and examine our works with careful inquiry. Perhaps by arguing with God he means that whoever obeyed God's commandments here will come with Him as a judge when He judges the people (Mt 19:28)... Therefore the Lord also says through Isaiah: "Relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. Come now, and let us reason together" (Isa 1:17-18).

13.2.6.en: For it is right that they should plead with God concerning the charges in the judgment, those who at (hearing) the words of God utterly renounce the present world. Thus speaking with Him is fulfilled by prayer, and pleading with Him by judgment.

13.2.7.en: Therefore the saint speaks here with the Almighty, so that he may afterward plead with Him (at the time of the general judgment), when he comes afterward with God as a judge, he who clings to the Almighty here by prayer.

13.2.8.en: As for the holy Church, to which we said before that Job bears a likeness that is to come, she not only judges the wicked when the time of the final judgment arrives, but even now does not cease to judge all, whether those who walk in evil or those who think foolishly.

13.3.0.en: 4 "But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value. 5 O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom. 6 Hear now my reasoning, and hearken to the pleadings of my lips. 7 Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him? 8 Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God?"

13.3.1.en: But ye are forgers of lies,

13.3.2.en: ye are all physicians of no value [4].

13.3.3.en: Job complains of his friends, because they judged him and condemned him according to their false notions and their lack of understanding of God's providence and care and His plan for mankind. Therefore they became forgers of lies. They uttered falsehood and fabricated false accusations against him.

13.3.4.en: They came to him as physicians to attend to his wounds, but in truth they were physicians of no value; they did not know the disease, so the treatment turned out deadly. They changed from wise physicians into charlatan quacks. They claimed science and knowledge, while in complete ignorance of the divine truth, because they had lost love.

13.3.5.en: Job did not accept his brothers as physicians offering him the cure, looking instead to the coming Messiah, as the heavenly Physician of souls and bodies, who heals the eyes of our souls so that they enjoy the vision of divine things.

13.3.6.en: Wonderful is our heavenly Physician, for when He declared Himself a physician He was eating in the house of a tax collector, with many tax collectors and sinners gathered around Him. He did not preach to them nor rebuke them for their sins, but He ate with them (Lk 5:27-32). I do not think I would find a doctor who enters a hospital and invites all the patients to eat with him, then leaves them and goes out of the hospital without giving them medicines specific to their diseases to heal them.

13.3.7.en: The Lord gave the medicine when He ate with them, for He gave them practical love; He ate with those whom society loathed and did not even want to deal with, lest it be defiled. The Holy One stretches out His hand and eats with them, so that they may realize that their Savior is not far from them, nor aloof from them. This is the heavenly medicine that the heavenly Physician offered. He is a unique Physician and His medicine is unique!

13.3.8.en: And the wonder is that He declared His person thus as a physician at the very moments when He declared that His disciples are the children of the bridechamber, or friends of the Bridegroom. As though those who work with Him have as their work to receive the mysteries of the Bridegroom, so as to proclaim His person, His characteristics and His abilities to the bride: the humanity that accepts faith in Him. As though those who work with the Physician have no work except preparing for the joyful heavenly wedding.

13.3.9.en: The work of the servant of the Lord Christ, and of all leaders, indeed of every Christian, is to contribute to the preparation for this wedding, not by rebuke, reproof and condemnation, but by revealing the love of the Bridegroom and His coming down to His bride, and opening the doors of heaven, her bridal chamber, to her. For the bride is prepared for her Bridegroom by discovering her Bridegroom's love for her and His longing for her.

13.3.10.en: * You are harmful physicians who renew the diseases, [you renew evil], you who do not bring healing from the wounds by using very fitting remedies. So you think that you are defending God, and that your mouth utters pleasing words; yet you see evils in the one placed on trial, and you come to help the enemy by stirring up feelings of pain in the wounded.

13.3.11.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The heavenly Guide, the Logos, is called the Leader when He calls mankind to salvation... But when He works as a physician or trainer, His name becomes "the Instructor"... For the sick soul needs an instructor who heals its passions. Then it needs the Teacher who gives it understanding... "the revelation of the Logos." Thus, since the Logos wishes our salvation step by step, He uses an excellent method: at first He leads, then He corrects, and finally He teaches.

13.3.12.en: * Who is He? Learn briefly that He is the Word of truth, the Word of incorruption, who renews man by restoring him to the truth. He is the goad that urges to salvation. He is the destroyer of perdition and the driver away of death. He builds the temple of God in men, taking them for God as a dwelling.

13.3.13.en: The sick need a savior, the lost need a guide, the blind need one who leads them to the light, the thirsty need the living fountain from which whoever drinks will never thirst, the dead need life, the sheep need a shepherd, and children need a teacher; all mankind needs Jesus!

13.3.14.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Blessed indeed are those who in their need of the Son of God have gone beyond the need of Him as a physician to heal their diseases, or as a shepherd, or as a redeemer, and whose need of Him has become need of Him as Wisdom and as Logos, or as one of the other titles He offers to those who have the spiritual Pascha that prepares them for the highest graces.

13.3.15.en: * Within the divinity of the Word there is power, not only to help and heal those who are sick..., but to reveal mysteries to those who are pure in body and mind.

13.3.16.en: The Word was sent as a physician to sinners, and also as a teacher to those who are already pure and without sin.

13.3.17.en: * By the light of the Word the darkness of heretical teachings is dispelled. For the Word opens the eyes of our souls, so that we can distinguish between light and darkness, and in every case choose to remain in the light.

13.3.18.en: * He who seeks healing has no course but to follow Jesus.

13.3.19.en: * Come now to Jesus, the heavenly Physician.

13.3.20.en: Enter this clinic, which is His Church.

13.3.21.en: Look. There lie great numbers of the weak. You find a woman seeking cleansing (Mk 5:25; Lev 12). You also find a leper isolated "without the camp" because of the defilement of his leprosy (Mk 1:40; Lev 13:46).

13.3.22.en: They seek healing from the Physician, asking how they may become healthy and how they may be cleansed.

13.3.23.en: Jesus the Physician is Himself the Word of God. He prepares medicines for His patients, not from preparations of herbs, but from the holy things of words.

13.3.24.en: If someone looks at those medicines of words scattered without order in the folds of the books, and does not know the power of the individual words, he may perhaps turn from them as cheap things lacking eloquence. But he who knows that the medicine of souls is in Christ will certainly understand from these books that are read in the Church how every person must gather useful herbs from the fields and mountains, I mean the power of the words, so that he who is troubled in soul may obtain healing, not by the power of the outer branches (of medicinal plants) and the surface bark, so much as by the effectiveness of the inner sap.

13.3.25.en: * There are also many other things hidden from us, known only to Him who is the Physician of our souls. For as regards our bodily health, we find it sometimes necessary to take disagreeable and bitter medicines as a cure for diseases we have brought upon ourselves through food and drink. So it happens if the nature of the disease requires harsh treatment with the surgeon's knife in a painful operation. Yes, and if the disease happens to extend beyond the effect of these remedies, recourse is had in the end to where the disease must be cauterized with fire. How can we realize that God, our Physician, desires to wash away the diseases of our souls that many sins and crimes have brought upon us, and uses a corrective treatment of similar kinds that may extend to the point of imposing the punishment of fire on those who have lost the health of their souls.

13.3.26.en: Origen * First, that you may realize God's condescension. Condescend and be humble for your own sakes, looking to God who condescended in humility also for your sake and not for His own...

13.3.27.en: Confess your weakness; and lie before the Physician in patience.

13.3.28.en: When you realize His condescension you are lifted up with Him, not by His raising Himself as the Word, but rather by being understood by you more and more...

13.3.29.en: He does not increase, but you are the ones who advance, so that He is as one who has risen with you...

13.3.30.en: Look at the tree: it first sends its roots down so that it may grow upward. It fixes its lower root in the earth so that its top may extend to heaven. Does it make any effort to grow except through humility? Then "that Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love... might be filled with all the fulness of God" (Eph 3:17-19).

13.3.31.en: St. Augustine * We see that the Holy Scripture does not present the Lord to us under one name, nor only under the names assigned to His divinity or indicating His greatness; sometimes it uses the distinctions of nature (His hypostatic properties), and knows to say: [the name which is above every name] (Phil 2:9), the name of the Son, and the true Son, and the only-begotten God the Son, and the power of God and His wisdom and His Word. And sometimes, considering the multitude of ways by which grace comes to us, which in His goodness He grants to those who seek it according to His wisdom of many aspects, Scripture calls Him by many other titles. It calls Him at one time the Shepherd, at another the King, then the Physician, the Bridegroom, the Way, the Door, the Fountain, the Bread, the Axe and the Rock. These names do not indicate the nature, as I said, but the multiplicity of the activity that He exerts, out of mercy to each one of His creatures, and in answer to the need of everyone who asks Him.

13.3.32.en: St. Basil the Great * There is one Physician, who is at the same time flesh and spirit (man and God), begotten γεννητός: gennetos, and unbegotten, God become man. True life in death (in a mortal body), He was mortal (in the flesh) and is now immortal (by His resurrection), of Mary and of God, He is Jesus Christ our Lord.

13.3.33.en: St. Ignatius Theophorus * Let us then worship Him as God, believing in His becoming man, for what profit is there in saying of Him that He is a man and not God, or what salvation is there for us if we refuse to confess His humanity along with His divinity? Let us confess His presence, for He is King and Physician. For Jesus the King, having become a Physician, girded Himself with the linen of our humanity, and healed what was sick. The perfect Teacher of babes became a babe among them (Rom 2:20), that He might give wisdom to the foolish. The Bread of heaven came down to earth to feed the hungry!

13.3.34.en: * "Jesus" means "Savior," but in Greek it means "the Healer," for He is the Physician of souls and bodies, the Healer of spirits; He opened the eyes of the man born blind, and led minds to the light. He heals the visibly lame, and leads sinners in the way of repentance. He says to the paralytic: "Sin no more," and also: "Take up thy bed, and walk," because the body was paralyzed because of the sin of the soul. He served the soul first so that He might extend healing to the body.

13.3.35.en: Therefore if any of you is suffering in soul because of his sins, you will find Him a physician for you. And if any of you is of little faith, let him say to Him: "Help thou mine unbelief" (Mk 9:24).

13.3.36.en: And if any of you is afflicted with bodily pains, let him not be unbelieving, but draw near, for Jesus heals such diseases, and let him know that Jesus is the Christ.

13.3.37.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * By the Physician's many medicines He grants healing... He binds up the wounds with firm commandments, and sends forth warmth when He forgives sins. He pricks the heart as wine does, when He announces His judgment. And he set him on his own beast (Lk 10:34); consider how He lifts you up (in Himself), since He bore our sins and suffered for us (Isa 53:4). The Shepherd also carried the lost sheep on His shoulders (Lk 15:5).

13.3.38.en: St. Ambrose O that ye would altogether hold your peace!

13.4.0.en: and it should be your wisdom [5].

13.4.1.en: They came to offer wise counsels, yet it appeared that they themselves rather needed someone to guide them and bring them into wisdom. The wisdom they lacked was that they should altogether hold their peace; their silence is more beneficial than vain, wounding speech. As the wise man says: "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding" (Prov 17:28).

13.4.2.en: * [It would have been better, for God's sake, for you to keep silence, and it would be your wisdom] [5]... The wise man is not only one who speaks well, offering useful counsels and declaring what is beneficial and dignified for all, but also one who bridles himself (Jas 3:2)... He observes what David sang in the Psalms: [Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity] (Ps 141:3-4).

13.4.3.en: Let us withdraw completely from them, even if they sometimes think they are defending God, not with the intention of glorifying God, but to slander the one who dedicates himself to righteousness and to betray the soldier of goodness... For a man needs to flee from deceivers and their friendship, and turn his face away from their flattery. But men of goodness accept the rebuke that comes from them, and remember with dignity their malicious talk against them, for all things turn to their good and work for good (Rom 8:28), and soon they receive the praise of God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit...

13.4.4.en: Job spoke, after losing all his wealth, as though he were in abundance.

13.4.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * As in a house, when the door is shut, it is not known which members are hidden in it, so in general, if the fool keeps his peace (his silence), he hides whether he is wise or foolish. So it is when no work comes into the light, the mind speaks even if the man is silent. Therefore the saint, seeing his companions appear as what they are not, commands them to keep their peace (their silence), so that they may not be exposed for what they are. Thus it was said of Solomon: "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise" (Prov 17:28).

13.4.7.en: * [Set a guard, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips] (Ps 141:3). He did not say "a fortified barrier," but [a fortified door]. A door is opened as well as shut. If this is a door, let it open and shut. It opens for the confession of sin, and shuts for the forgiveness of sin. For it is a door for protection, not for destruction.

13.5.0.en: St. Augustine Hear now my reasoning, and hearken to the pleadings of my lips [6].

13.5.1.en: He calls them to listen to him instead of vain talk. Although they did not interrupt him, they paid no attention to his words, nor did they give heed to the cries of his bitter soul. They thought they had defended God and spoken the truth, but without practical love they do not know God, nor do they perceive the truth.

13.5.2.en: * [Hear now my rebukes, and give ear to the judgment of my lips] [6]. Well does he begin first by offering rebuke and afterward "judgment." For unless the fool's pride is quenched, he cannot at all understand the judgment of the righteous.

13.6.0.en: Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him? [7]

13.6.1.en: Job mocks them because they thought that God needed them to defend Him and to reveal His justice. As though he says to them: Who are you, weak ones without love, that you should defend the divine truth, which is inseparable from love?

13.6.2.en: Under the pretext of defending divine justice they spoke deceit, and made false accusations against Job, and counted him wicked, and so fell into lying, cruelty, injustice and wronging their brother. And they justify all this by saying that it is "for God." They did not realize that "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20).

13.6.3.en: They justified their evil conduct toward Job as being to achieve a lofty aim, namely the defense of God. Does a good end justify an evil means? As though they were saying: "Let us do evil, that good may come" (Rom 3:8). God rebuked those who hate their brethren while they praise God: "Your brethren that hated you, that cast you out for my name's sake, said, Let the LORD be glorified: but he shall appear to your joy, and they shall be ashamed" (Isa 66:5).

13.6.4.en: He who has fellowship with God, the Truth, cannot practice deceit and lying, unless a man has turned aside from God, who cannot endure deceit. The Psalmist often puts deceit on the same level as the shedding of blood, because its aim is the destruction of the souls of others and their possessions or honor; and the deceiver destroys himself, and deprives himself of glory and eternal blessedness.

13.6.5.en: "Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man" (Ps 5:6).

13.6.6.en: "Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile" (Ps 32:2).

13.6.7.en: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile" (Ps 34:13).

13.6.8.en: "But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee" (Ps 55:23).

13.6.9.en: "He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight" (Ps 101:7).

13.6.10.en: "What doth he give thee? or what doth he add unto thee, thou deceitful tongue?" (Ps 120:3).

13.6.11.en: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Prov 11:1).

13.6.12.en: "The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward" (Prov 11:18).

13.6.13.en: "He that speaketh truth sheweth forth righteousness: but a false witness deceit" (Prov 12:17).

13.6.14.en: "Deceit is in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace is joy" (Prov 12:20).

13.6.15.en: "The wisdom of the prudent is to understand his way: but the folly of fools is deceit" (Prov 14:8).

13.6.16.en: "A true witness delivereth souls: but he that speaketh lies is deceit" (Prov 14:25).

13.6.17.en: "Weight and weight is an abomination to the LORD, and deceitful balances are not good" (Prov 20:23).

13.6.18.en: "The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with a wicked mind" (Prov 21:27).

13.6.19.en: "He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him" (Prov 26:24).

13.6.20.en: "For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and remove from thoughts that are without understanding, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in" (Wis 1:5).

13.6.21.en: "Yea, speedily was he taken away, lest that wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul" (Wis 4:11).

13.6.22.en: "Bring not every man into thine house: for the deceitful man hath many trains" (Sir 11:31).

13.6.23.en: *Do you not speak before the Lord, and utter deceit before Him, despite your splendid words? This is what he wishes to say: you do not believe that God listens to what you say, because deceit dictates your dialogue. No good motive moves you, but the desire to harm my reputation and to make wounding comments. For even if your words are proper, you do not express a good intention by them; they do not seek correction, reform and progress, but seek destruction, for you are not teaching a man who is wholly ignorant.

13.6.24.en: St. John Chrysostom * [Hath God need of your lie, that ye speak deceitfully for him?] God has no need of a lie, for the truth does not accept being accomplished with the help of falsehood... The heretics speak deceit for Him, deceiving those of weak minds, misleading their concepts of God in a foolish manner.

13.6.26.en: In St. Augustine's commentary on (Ps 55:23), he compares the shedders of blood with the deceiving heretics and those who speak deceit, and says that the shedders of blood are manifest murderers who shed the blood of bodies and do not kill souls, whereas the heretics destroy souls and shed their invisible blood. They are bloody and deceitful men!

13.6.27.en: In his commentary on the Psalmist's question and answer: [What doth he give thee, and what is set before thee against the deceitful tongue? Sharpened arrows of the mighty, with coals of desolation] (Ps 120:3-4), he sees that the opposition to those with deceitful tongues is not by mere words, but requires the word of God, the sharpened arrows of the mighty one, together with living examples of righteous persons who were like a lifeless, desolate desert and became burning like coals. He says: [It is not enough to answer them with words, but we also defend with examples... The word "coals" is used to express examples of many sinners who returned to the Lord. You hear people marveling and saying: "I know a man how addicted to drink he was, how base in his love of theaters and the circus and his love of deceit; now behold, he serves God, how innocent he has become!" Do not marvel, for he has become a living coal. Rejoice that he is alive, he for whom you grieved because he was dead.]

13.7.0.en: Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God? [8]

13.7.1.en: God does not need defenders; in their defense they hate their brothers. "Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God?" How do they serve God by hatred and loathing of their brothers? In their zeal for God, they insult God and rob Him of the seat of His judgment as the Judge of mankind. For He alone knows every soul and its strength and inclinations, and man's gifts, his biological makeup, his energies and the circumstances surrounding him. On the basis of all this He is the One who condemns or justifies. Truly we may know a man who committed a certain sin, perhaps obvious, needing no investigation; but can we judge the man as a whole because of a sin or sins he committed at one time, when we do not know his depths or his circumstances?!

13.7.2.en: * [Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God?] [8] For when fools see the deeds of the wise, they all appear to them to be worthy of blame. They forget their own emptiness and shortcomings, and judge the conduct of others with greater zeal... On the other hand, when the righteous rebuke the conduct of the wicked, they always acknowledge their own weaknesses and that they themselves deserve blame. For even if they rebuke and rush strongly to resist the evils of others from outside, yet they sympathize with them inwardly, realizing that the examination of men's sins belongs to God... Therefore the friends of blessed Job rebuked his deeds as though they themselves had done nothing blameworthy.

13.7.3.en: Well was it said here: [Will ye accept his person? will ye contend for God?] For a person to put on the face of God means that he claims for himself His authority to condemn; and a person contends for God when he rebukes the weak points in others and does not feel his own inward weakness.

13.7.5.en: * An elder said: "If no one knows what is in a man save his spirit, as the Apostle says, and if we know that many have repented and we did not know of their repentance, then a man may repent at the end of his life, and be accepted like the repentance of the thief; so you must not judge anyone. For the Judge is God alone, so how can anyone dare to intervene in what belongs to God?!"

13.7.6.en: The Garden of the Monks * Do not be a judge of your brother, that you may be made worthy of forgiveness. Perhaps you always see him as wrong, but you do not know with what ending he departs the world. The thief crucified with Jesus was a murderer and a shedder of blood, and Judas was a disciple of Christ and among the intimates, since the purse was with him; yet in a short time they changed, so the thief entered Paradise, and the disciple deserved the gallows and perished.

13.7.7.en: St. Anastasius * Look, my brothers: the work of the servants at the wedding of the king's son (Mt 22) was nothing but drawing the good and the wicked to the feast. The Lord did not say of them that they judged those invited and distinguished between the good and the wicked, nor did He say of them that they found one who did not have a wedding garment; rather the king himself was the one who saw him, the master of the house alone discovered him and cast him out.

13.7.8.en: St. Augustine * If you see a man who has sinned and you see him on the morrow, do not look at him as a sinner, for you do not know whether in the period of your absence from him he has done something good after the fall; rather, plead with the Lord with sighs and bitter tears, entreating Him!

13.8.0.en: 9 "Is it good that he should search you out? or as one man is deceived, do ye deceive him? 10 He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons. 11 Shall not his excellency make you afraid? and his dread fall upon you? 12 Your speeches are like ashes, and your strongholds are strongholds of clay."

13.8.1.en: Is it good that he should search you out? or as one man is deceived, do ye deceive him? [9]

13.8.2.en: It is for their good, and better for them, that God should search their hearts and reveal to them their hatred of their brothers and their loathing of the truth, than that they should cloak themselves with an outward defense of God, and so deceive Him (beguile Him unawares) as a man is deceived.

13.8.3.en: * Every innovator is, in relation to God, "an enemy and a defender," for in his struggle and in the way of his defense of God he resists the truth. But nothing can escape the sight of God, for He judges according to the thoughts of the heart rather than the outward appearance in which he seems to be one who serves God.

13.8.5.en: * How do they resist the truth except by the vanity of their pride, exalted in vain? While they set themselves up on high as great and righteous men, they pass away like empty air.

13.8.6.en: St. Augustine * If anyone objects to the existence of heretics now, let him remember that it has been so from the beginning, since Satan was always setting up error over against the truth. In the beginning God promised good things, and Satan too made his promise. God established Paradise, and Satan deceived man by saying: [Ye shall be as gods] (Gen 3:5); for if he was unable to provide a work, he offered promises which are rather words, and this is the nature of deceivers.

13.8.7.en: After this came Cain, and with him Abel; the sons of Seth, and with them the daughters of men; Ham, and with him Japheth; Abraham (and in his days) there was Pharaoh; Jacob, and with him Esau.

13.8.8.en: And so came Moses (and Aaron), and the two magicians arose.

13.8.9.en: The prophets, and with them the false prophets.

13.8.10.en: The apostles and the false apostles; Christ, and the Antichrist will come.

13.8.11.en: This is what was before, and what has happened up to that day... In brief, there was never a time when falsehood did not exist to stand against the truth. So do not be troubled.

13.9.0.en: St. John Chrysostom He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons [10].

13.9.1.en: In rebuking Job in this spirit filled with hatred, they became respecters of persons, even if secretly; therefore they are not counted in the eyes of God worthy of praise, but of severe reproof. God abhors the hatred concealed under the defense of God and of His glory and Kingdom. Perhaps by respect of persons he meant that they used to honor him, perhaps with exaggeration, for his wealth, and for no reason their conduct completely changed when he became poor and lost his social position and his authority as a king or leader, and also all his money. Scripture has warned us against partiality.

13.9.2.en: "Wherefore now let the fear of the LORD be upon you; take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts" (2 Chr 19:7).

13.9.3.en: "These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment" (Prov 24:23).

13.9.4.en: "To have respect of persons is not good: for for a piece of bread that man will transgress" (Prov 28:21).

13.9.5.en: "For there is no respect of persons with God" (Rom 2:11).

13.9.6.en: "And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him" (Eph 6:9).

13.9.7.en: "But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons" (Col 3:25).

13.9.8.en: "I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality" (1 Tim 5:21).

13.9.9.en: "My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons" (Jas 2:1).

13.9.10.en: "And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear" (1 Pet 1:17).

13.9.11.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) says that God is the searcher of the secrets of hearts and nothing is hidden from Him (1 Cor 4:5); for it may happen that under the cover of defending the truth, some blame the righteous man, and show partiality to those who stand against the righteous, while they stand on the side of those who blaspheme God. These claim that they glorify God, while they bear no sincerity in their conduct. They are like the demons who said to the Lord Christ: [Thou art the Son of God] (Mk 3:11); in this they do not seek His glory, but are terrified of what will come upon them.

13.9.12.en: * What benefit comes to you from honoring (showing partiality to) the rich man? Is it because he is better prepared to keep the love of others for him? So we do kindness to those from whom we expect that they will repay us for it. We must think rather of the weak and needy, because for the sake of these we hope for recompense from the Lord Jesus, who in the example of the wedding feast (Lk 14:12-13) gave us a general picture of virtue. For He asked us to give our works rather to those who are not able to repay us.

13.9.13.en: * If the Kingdom of God is for the poor, who is richer than they?

13.9.14.en: St. Ambrose * All are equal before God; only the rank of each is raised according to his faith, and not according to his money.

13.9.15.en: St. Augustine * Many rebuke me, saying: You are always pressing hard on the rich, and they in turn press hard on the poor.

13.9.16.en: Well, I do press hard on the rich, or rather not on the rich, but on those who misuse money. I do not attack their persons but their greed. Wealth is one thing, and greed is another; having a surplus is one thing, and covetousness is another.

13.9.17.en: Are you rich? I do not forbid you this. Be rich. Are you greedy? I warn you... I will not be silent.

13.9.18.en: Do you attack me because of this? I am ready for my blood to be shed, but I want to keep you from sinning. I bear you no hatred, nor do I wage war on you, but I want one thing only, the benefit of those who listen to me.

13.9.19.en: The rich are my children, and the poor are also my children. One womb (Baptism) brought them forth in great travail. All are the offspring of her who travailed with them. So if you heap insults on the poor man, I warn you, because the poor man in this case suffers no loss like yours. For he does not fall into error; the loss that befalls him is merely the loss of money, whereas you, as a rich man, suffer loss in your spirit.

13.10.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Shall not his excellency make you afraid? and his dread fall upon you? [11]

13.10.1.en: Job warns them about their improper conduct, for while they think they are defending God, they fall under His wrath, because they walk in evil, and the awe of His majesty and His dread fall upon them.

13.10.2.en: * Now the righteous perceive the awe of God before His wrath is stirred up against them. They fear Him while He is calm (toward them), lest they be compelled to feel Him when He moves in anger. On the other hand, the wicked are terrified of Him for the first time when they are struck with the rod, and terror raises them from the sleep of their torpor, as vengeance disturbs them. So it was said by the prophet: [Vexation alone will be the support for understanding what they hear] (cf. Isa 28:19). For when they begin to fall under the blows of vengeance because of their contempt for God's commandments and their neglect of them, they understand what they hear. The Psalmist says: "When he slew them, then they sought him" (Ps 78:34)...

13.11.0.en: Your speeches are like ashes, and your strongholds are strongholds of clay! [12]

13.11.1.en: Job's friends boasted that they were defenders of God and His justice and His judgments, and behold all their talk is like ashes, trifling and worthless; the wind blows and the ashes vanish. Their thoughts fly away from their earthy bodies; they pass away, and their human wisdom passes with them. They do not heap up wisdom for time, but heaps of clay, from which the children of God want deliverance.

13.11.2.en: He likens their talk to dust, because it rests on earthly, transient thoughts, and does not depend on heavenly, eternal wisdom. They fortify themselves with human logic, which cannot protect them except for moments.

13.11.3.en: * [Their remembrance is like ashes] [12]. All who are shaped by the present condition have earthly thoughts, for in all they do they leave a temporary memorial of themselves in the world. Some strive in war, others by erecting towering buildings, and some by recording books that bear the experiences of this world. They toil and struggle and build in order to set up a memorial to their names. But since life runs swiftly toward its end, what can endure in it, when nature itself is swiftly falling away?

13.11.4.en: A breath of wind scatters the ashes, as it is written: "The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away" (Ps 1:4). Rightly the remembrance of the foolish is compared to ashes, since its place is to be scattered by a breath of wind. The more a man toils to gain glory for his name, the more he places his remembrance, which is like ashes, in the gusts of the winds of mortality that hasten to a moment. In contrast to this it is written of the righteous: "The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance" (Ps 112:6). For by the very circumstances in which he impresses his works on the eyes of God alone, his name remains fixed for his remembrance in the eternal world.

13.11.5.en: * [And your bodies to bodies of clay] [12]... Thus the neck is brought down to clay, when every proud man goes down to death, and the body that was lifted up in corruption is dissolved. Let us consider the corpses of the rich lying in their graves, what kind of death has come upon the lifeless body, what is the stench of its corruption!

13.12.0.en: Hold your peace from me, that I may speak, and let come on me what may [13].

13.12.1.en: If Job was struck with trials of this magnitude, they are lighter than what befell him from the words of his friends. His trials will not condemn him but vindicate him, whereas their wicked words, their lying and their hatred are greater misfortunes than any disaster or calamity!

13.12.2.en: It is fitting for them to be silent, for they are lovers of profitless dispute. Let Job speak, and reveal to them what they are, even if he speaks while sitting on the dunghill, wearing a garment of the worms around him.

13.12.3.en: Job does not care what befalls him: "and let come on me what may," and however they interpret these calamities, and think the worst of him, all this will not stop the testimony of his conscience, which he gives with all uprightness and integrity.

13.12.4.en: * [Hold your peace from me a little, that I may speak what my mind dictates to me] [13]. It appears that they spoke with a fleshly understanding, those whom he requires to be silent, so that he may speak as his mind dictates to him. As though he says in plain words: I do not speak in a fleshly manner but spiritually, for I hear with spiritual understanding the things that I present through the service of the flesh.

13.12.6.en: * When you meet a man who loves disputes and begins to argue with you about what is self-evident and true, cut off the conversation and withdraw quickly, for his mind has turned to stone.

13.12.7.en: For as water spoils the finest wines, so foolish discussions spoil those who are virtuous in their conduct and in their characters.

13.13.0.en: 14 "Wherefore do I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in mine hand? 15 Behold, he slayeth me; I have no hope: only I will justify my way before him. 16 This also shall be my salvation, that the ungodly shall not come before him. 17 Hear diligently my words, and my declaration in your ears. 18 Behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified. 19 Who is he that will contend with me, that now I should hold my peace and give up the ghost?"

13.13.1.en: Wherefore do I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in mine hand? [14]

13.13.2.en: Perhaps Job wishes to bring out his desire to bear witness to the truth under all circumstances, not only when he was torn by his calamities, but even if he tore his body with his teeth, and put his life on his palm to hand it over to death; all this will not make him silent about revealing his innocence in the Lord, and about his friends' wrong interpretation of the events.

13.13.3.en: * It means: why should I condemn myself severely before men, or show what my heart inclines to, since there is no edification of my neighbor in this, whether by condemning my evils or by displaying my good?

13.13.5.en: * He says: I am like those who find consolation in devouring themselves; like those who bite their bodies hard, experiencing a kind of relief of their pains; this is what happens with me when I express myself in this way.

13.13.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * This is the reason that he takes his flesh in his teeth, their vain, provoking words. He speaks in anger, and wants to calm himself.

13.13.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the teeth here refer to the inner senses, which chew what occupies the mind and present it to the belly of memory. [Therefore it was rightly said: "Every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge" (Jer 31:30). What is the sour grape but sin? The sour grape is fruit before its time. So whoever desires to be satisfied with the pleasures of the present life is like one who hastens to eat fruit before its time. Therefore the teeth of him who eats the sour grape are set on edge, that is, while he feeds on the delight of the present life he has perceptions unable to eat, that is, unable to perceive spiritual things. For the same reason, since they delight in outward things they become dull of sense with regard to inward things, and while the soul feeds on sin it is unable to eat the bread of righteousness. And since the teeth are bound to the habit of sin, they will not be able to chew that goodness so as to listen within.]

13.13.8.en: As though Job, wishing to take outward things (his flesh) in spiritual meanings, chews them with the teeth of his spirit to enjoy the spiritual pleasures that his friends do not accept, because they seek the glory of the world and the pleasures of the flesh. They oppose him and seek his destruction, for the carnal cannot endure the spiritual.
